LESSON 26 OF 106·Cryptography Essentials

What Cryptography Actually Promises (and What It Doesn't)

Cryptography is a tool with a threat model, not magic: confidentiality, integrity and authenticity are conditional guarantees, and the rest of the system decides whether they hold.

Foundation11 min
Why this matters

Cryptography reliably does a few specific things and reliably does not do the others. Most real cryptographic failures come from asking it for something it was never designed to provide.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Encryption provides confidentiality, and it does so only for readers holding the key.
  • A cryptographic hash provides integrity by making any change detectable, and it is a one-way function rather than an encryption.
  • A digital signature provides authenticity and non-repudiation, using a private key to sign and a public key to verify.
  • A key agreement protocol lets two parties derive a shared secret over a channel that may already be observed, which is what TLS relies on.
  • None of these provide correctness of the input, safety of the software using them, or proof that the person holding a key deserves it.

The background

  • Classical cryptography was used for centuries before computing, and was traditionally about concealing a message rather than proving anything.
  • The introduction of public-key cryptography in the 1970s changed what was possible, because key distribution no longer required a private channel.
  • Formal security proofs arrived in the 1990s, replacing an assumption that a scheme was secure because nobody had broken it.
  • Practical guidance is now published as standards that specify exactly which construction to use, because the number of insecure choices is very large.

Real-world examples

  • An encrypted connection is still wrong if the software on either end has a flaw, since cryptography only protects the channel.
  • A correctly signed message does not mean the action requested is safe, only that it genuinely came from the claimed sender.
  • A hash matching proves the file is unchanged since hashing, not that the file is safe to run.

What to look for

  • Decide which property you actually need: confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, or all three.
  • Check that a construction is being used for the purpose it was designed for rather than a similar-sounding one.
  • Notice when a random value is reused, since that breaks several otherwise-sound schemes.
  • Treat any custom or home-grown cryptographic design as a serious finding.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

SP 800-175A — Guideline for Using Cryptographic Standards

Reading how a national standards body scopes what cryptography is expected to deliver in a system, and which decisions it insists are made in writing

Open NIST resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Use well-reviewed, standard constructions rather than designing your own.
  • Prefer high-level libraries over interfaces that expose raw choices you have to get right.
  • State the security goal in a document, so a reviewer can tell whether the design meets it.
  • Budget time for algorithm migration, since old schemes stop being safe long before they stop working.
